name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_BREATHINGANDEXCHANGEOFGASES_MATCH_Q01 - Respiratory organs across different animal groups

questiontext.text:
Match the animal groups in List I with their respective respiratory organs/modes of gas exchange in List II:

List I (Animal Group)List II (Respiratory Organ / Mode)
A. Sponges and flatworms(i) Moist cuticle
B. Earthworms(ii) Network of tracheal tubes
C. Insects(iii) Simple diffusion over entire body surface
D. Aquatic arthropods and molluscs(iv) Gills (branchial respiration)

Choose the correct match from the options given below:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Mechanisms of breathing vary among animal groups depending primarily on their habitats and levels of organisation.

Step 2: Evaluation of Each Pair
- Lower invertebrates such as sponges, coelenterates, and flatworms exchange \(\mathrm{O_2}\) with \(\mathrm{CO_2}\) by simple diffusion over their entire body surface, so A pairs with (iii).
- Earthworms use their moist cuticle for gaseous exchange, so B pairs with (i).
- Insects possess a network of tubes (tracheal tubes) to transport atmospheric air within the body, so C pairs with (ii).
- Most aquatic arthropods and molluscs use special vascularised structures called gills (branchial respiration), so D pairs with (iv).

Step 3: Final Conclusion
The correct matching is A–(iii), B–(i), C–(ii), D–(iv).

questiontext.text:
Match the human respiratory structures in List I with their characteristic descriptions in List II:

List I (Structure)List II (Characteristic)
A. Pharynx(i) Cartilaginous box that helps in sound production
B. Larynx(ii) Straight tube dividing at the 5th thoracic vertebra
C. Epiglottis(iii) Common passage for food and air
D. Trachea(iv) Thin elastic cartilaginous flap covering the glottis

Choose the correct match from the options given below:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
The conducting pathway of the human respiratory system consists of specialised anatomical structures that route air to the lungs while protecting the airway.

Step 2: Evaluation of Each Pair
- The nasal chamber opens into the pharynx, a portion of which serves as the common passage for food and air, so A pairs with (iii).
- The larynx is a cartilaginous box that helps in sound production and is called the sound box, so B pairs with (i).
- The epiglottis is a thin elastic cartilaginous flap that covers the glottis during swallowing to prevent food entry, so C pairs with (iv).
- The trachea is a straight tube extending up to the mid-thoracic cavity that divides at the level of the 5th thoracic vertebra into right and left primary bronchi, so D pairs with (ii).

Step 3: Final Conclusion
The correct matching is A–(iii), B–(i), C–(iv), D–(ii).

questiontext.text:
Match the respiratory volumes in List I with their average values in a healthy human in List II:

List I (Respiratory Volume)List II (Average Value)
A. Tidal Volume (TV)(i) \(1000\text{ mL to }1100\text{ mL}\)
B. Inspiratory Reserve Volume (IRV)(ii) \(500\text{ mL}\)
C. Expiratory Reserve Volume (ERV)(iii) \(1100\text{ mL to }1200\text{ mL}\)
D. Residual Volume (RV)(iv) \(2500\text{ mL to }3000\text{ mL}\)

Choose the correct match from the options given below:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Standard respiratory volumes represent specific quantities of air moved during normal or forced breathing, or retained in the lungs, and are measured clinically using a spirometer.

Step 2: Evaluation of Each Pair
- Tidal Volume (TV) is the volume of air inspired or expired during normal respiration, approximately \(500\text{ mL}\), so A pairs with (ii).
- Inspiratory Reserve Volume (IRV) is the additional volume inspired by forcible inspiration, averaging \(2500\text{ mL to }3000\text{ mL}\), so B pairs with (iv).
- Expiratory Reserve Volume (ERV) is the additional volume expired by forcible expiration, averaging \(1000\text{ mL to }1100\text{ mL}\), so C pairs with (i).
- Residual Volume (RV) is the volume of air remaining in the lungs even after a forcible expiration, averaging \(1100\text{ mL to }1200\text{ mL}\), so D pairs with (iii).

Step 3: Final Conclusion
The correct matching is A–(ii), B–(iv), C–(i), D–(iii).

questiontext.text:
Match the pulmonary capacities in List I with their corresponding combinations of respiratory volumes in List II:

List I (Pulmonary Capacity)List II (Volume Expression)
A. Inspiratory Capacity (IC)(i) \(\mathrm{ERV} + \mathrm{RV}\)
B. Expiratory Capacity (EC)(ii) \(\mathrm{ERV} + \mathrm{TV} + \mathrm{IRV}\)
C. Functional Residual Capacity (FRC)(iii) \(\mathrm{TV} + \mathrm{IRV}\)
D. Vital Capacity (VC)(iv) \(\mathrm{TV} + \mathrm{ERV}\)

Choose the correct match from the options given below:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Pulmonary capacities are derived by adding two or more basic respiratory volumes for clinical diagnosis of lung function.

Step 2: Evaluation of Each Pair
- Inspiratory Capacity (IC) is the total volume inspired after a normal expiration, which equals \(\mathrm{TV} + \mathrm{IRV}\), so A pairs with (iii).
- Expiratory Capacity (EC) is the total volume expired after a normal inspiration, which equals \(\mathrm{TV} + \mathrm{ERV}\), so B pairs with (iv).
- Functional Residual Capacity (FRC) is the volume of air remaining in the lungs after a normal expiration, which equals \(\mathrm{ERV} + \mathrm{RV}\), so C pairs with (i).
- Vital Capacity (VC) is the maximum volume of air a person can breathe in after a forced expiration (or breathe out after a forced inspiration), which equals \(\mathrm{ERV} + \mathrm{TV} + \mathrm{IRV}\), so D pairs with (ii).

Step 3: Final Conclusion
The correct matching is A–(iii), B–(iv), C–(i), D–(ii).

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_BREATHINGANDEXCHANGEOFGASES_MATCH_Q05 - Partial pressures of oxygen and carbon dioxide

questiontext.text:
Match the respiratory sites/compartments in List I with their respective partial pressures (in mm Hg) of \(\mathrm{O_2}\) and \(\mathrm{CO_2}\) in List II:

List I (Site / Compartment)List II (\(p\mathrm{O_2}\), \(p\mathrm{CO_2}\) in mm Hg)
A. Atmospheric air(i) \(p\mathrm{O_2} = 104\), \(p\mathrm{CO_2} = 40\)
B. Alveoli(ii) \(p\mathrm{O_2} = 159\), \(p\mathrm{CO_2} = 0.3\)
C. Oxygenated blood(iii) \(p\mathrm{O_2} = 40\), \(p\mathrm{CO_2} = 45\)
D. Deoxygenated blood(iv) \(p\mathrm{O_2} = 95\), \(p\mathrm{CO_2} = 40\)

Choose the correct match from the options given below:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Gases diffuse across membranes from regions of higher partial pressure to regions of lower partial pressure. Oxygen diffuses from atmosphere to alveoli, to blood, and finally to tissues, whereas carbon dioxide diffuses in the opposite direction.

Step 2: Evaluation of Each Pair
- Atmospheric air has the highest \(p\mathrm{O_2}\) (\(159\text{ mm Hg}\)) and lowest \(p\mathrm{CO_2}\) (\(0.3\text{ mm Hg}\)), so A pairs with (ii).
- Alveolar air has \(p\mathrm{O_2} = 104\text{ mm Hg}\) and \(p\mathrm{CO_2} = 40\text{ mm Hg}\), so B pairs with (i).
- Oxygenated blood leaving the alveoli has \(p\mathrm{O_2} = 95\text{ mm Hg}\) and \(p\mathrm{CO_2} = 40\text{ mm Hg}\), so C pairs with (iv).
- Deoxygenated blood returning from tissues has \(p\mathrm{O_2} = 40\text{ mm Hg}\) and \(p\mathrm{CO_2} = 45\text{ mm Hg}\), so D pairs with (iii).

Step 3: Final Conclusion
The correct matching is A–(ii), B–(i), C–(iv), D–(iii).

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_BREATHINGANDEXCHANGEOFGASES_MATCH_Q06 - Proportions of oxygen and carbon dioxide transport

questiontext.text:
Match the gas transport mechanisms in List I with their approximate percentage contribution in human blood in List II:

List I (Transport Mechanism)List II (Percentage)
A. \(\mathrm{O_2}\) transported by RBCs(i) Nearly \(70\%\)
B. \(\mathrm{O_2}\) carried in dissolved state in plasma(ii) About \(20\text{–}25\%\)
C. \(\mathrm{CO_2}\) carried as bicarbonate(iii) About \(97\%\)
D. \(\mathrm{CO_2}\) transported by RBCs as carbamino-haemoglobin(iv) About \(3\%\)

Choose the correct match from the options given below:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Blood transports \(\mathrm{O_2}\) and \(\mathrm{CO_2}\) in both chemically bound and physically dissolved forms.

Step 2: Evaluation of Each Pair
- About \(97\%\) of \(\mathrm{O_2}\) is transported by RBCs as oxyhaemoglobin, so A pairs with (iii).
- The remaining \(3\%\) of \(\mathrm{O_2}\) is carried in a dissolved state through plasma, so B pairs with (iv).
- Nearly \(70\%\) of \(\mathrm{CO_2}\) is carried in the form of bicarbonate ions (\(\mathrm{HCO_3^-}\)), so C pairs with (i).
- About \(20\text{–}25\%\) of \(\mathrm{CO_2}\) is transported by RBCs bound to haemoglobin as carbamino-haemoglobin (with the remaining \(\sim 7\%\) dissolved in plasma), so D pairs with (ii).

Step 3: Final Conclusion
The correct matching is A–(iii), B–(iv), C–(i), D–(ii).

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_BREATHINGANDEXCHANGEOFGASES_MATCH_Q07 - Breathing mechanics and physiological gas delivery

questiontext.text:
Match the physiological events/quantities in List I with their corresponding mechanisms/values under normal conditions in List II:

List I (Event / Quantity)List II (Mechanism / Value)
A. Increase in thoracic volume in antero-posterior axis(i) Approximately \(4\text{ mL}\) to alveoli
B. Increase in thoracic volume in dorso-ventral axis(ii) Contraction of diaphragm
C. \(\mathrm{O_2}\) delivered per \(100\text{ mL}\) of oxygenated blood(iii) Contraction of external intercostal muscles
D. \(\mathrm{CO_2}\) delivered per \(100\text{ mL}\) of deoxygenated blood(iv) Around \(5\text{ mL}\) to tissues

Choose the correct match from the options given below:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Inspiration expands the thoracic chamber along two perpendicular axes via distinct respiratory muscles, while blood delivers specific physiological volumes of \(\mathrm{O_2}\) and \(\mathrm{CO_2}\) per \(100\text{ mL}\) at the tissues and alveoli, respectively.

Step 2: Evaluation of Each Pair
- Contraction of the diaphragm increases the volume of the thoracic chamber in the antero-posterior axis, so A pairs with (ii).
- Contraction of the external intercostal muscles lifts up the ribs and sternum, increasing thoracic volume in the dorso-ventral axis, so B pairs with (iii).
- Under normal physiological conditions, every \(100\text{ mL}\) of oxygenated blood delivers around \(5\text{ mL}\) of \(\mathrm{O_2}\) to the tissues, so C pairs with (iv).
- Every \(100\text{ mL}\) of deoxygenated blood delivers approximately \(4\text{ mL}\) of \(\mathrm{CO_2}\) to the alveoli, so D pairs with (i).

Step 3: Final Conclusion
The correct matching is A–(ii), B–(iii), C–(iv), D–(i).

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_BREATHINGANDEXCHANGEOFGASES_MATCH_Q08 - Neural and chemical centres regulating respiration

questiontext.text:
Match the respiratory regulatory centres/receptors in List I with their locations and functions in List II:

List I (Regulatory Component)List II (Location and Function)
A. Respiratory rhythm centre(i) Pons region; reduces duration of inspiration
B. Pneumotaxic centre(ii) Medulla region; primarily maintains respiratory rhythm
C. Chemosensitive area(iii) Peripheral receptors detecting \(\mathrm{CO_2}\) and \(\mathrm{H^+}\) changes
D. Aortic arch and carotid artery receptors(iv) Adjacent to rhythm centre; highly sensitive to \(\mathrm{CO_2}\) and \(\mathrm{H^+}\)

Choose the correct match from the options given below:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Human respiratory rhythm is maintained and moderated by neural centres in the medulla and pons, modulated by central and peripheral chemoreceptors sensitive to \(\mathrm{CO_2}\) and \(\mathrm{H^+}\).

Step 2: Evaluation of Each Pair
- The respiratory rhythm centre is a specialised centre located in the medulla region of the brain, primarily responsible for maintaining respiratory rhythm, so A pairs with (ii).
- The pneumotaxic centre is located in the pons region of the brain; neural signals from it reduce the duration of inspiration and alter respiratory rate, so B pairs with (i).
- The chemosensitive area is situated adjacent to the rhythm centre in the medulla and is highly sensitive to \(\mathrm{CO_2}\) and hydrogen ions, so C pairs with (iv).
- Receptors associated with the aortic arch and carotid artery are peripheral chemoreceptors that recognise changes in \(\mathrm{CO_2}\) and \(\mathrm{H^+}\) concentration and signal the rhythm centre, so D pairs with (iii).

Step 3: Final Conclusion
The correct matching is A–(ii), B–(i), C–(iv), D–(iii).

questiontext.text:
Match the respiratory disorders/conditions in List I with their characteristic pathological features in List II:

List I (Condition / Disorder)List II (Pathological Feature)
A. Asthma(i) Chronic damage to alveolar walls decreasing respiratory surface
B. Emphysema(ii) Proliferation of fibrous tissues due to long dust exposure
C. Occupational respiratory disorder(iii) Inflammation of bronchi and bronchioles causing wheezing
D. Alveolar diffusion membrane(iv) Three-layered barrier of total thickness less than \(1\text{ mm}\)

Choose the correct match from the options given below:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Respiratory disorders impair specific structural components of the airway or gas-exchange barrier, reducing ventilatory efficiency or diffusion capacity.

Step 2: Evaluation of Each Pair
- Asthma is characterised by difficulty in breathing causing wheezing due to inflammation of the bronchi and bronchioles, so A pairs with (iii).
- Emphysema is a chronic disorder in which alveolar walls are damaged, decreasing the respiratory surface, so B pairs with (i).
- Occupational respiratory disorders arise in dust-intensive industries (such as grinding or stone-breaking), where prolonged exposure causes inflammation leading to fibrosis (proliferation of fibrous tissues), so C pairs with (ii).
- The alveolar diffusion membrane is a three-layered barrier (alveolar squamous epithelium, basement substance, and capillary endothelium) with a total thickness much less than \(1\text{ mm}\), so D pairs with (iv).

Step 3: Final Conclusion
The correct matching is A–(iii), B–(i), C–(ii), D–(iv).
